pp:ec:2009:q3.title: GATE EC 2009 | Set 1 | Question: 3
pp:ec:2009:q3.question: A function is given by $f(t)=sin^{2}t+cos2t$. Which of the following is true ?
options: f has frequency components at 0 and $\frac{1}{2\pi } Hz$
f has frequency components at 0 and $\frac{1}{\pi } Hz$
f has frequency components at $\frac{1}{2\pi } \; and \; \frac{1}{\pi}Hz$
f has frequency components at 0, $\frac{1}{2\pi } \; and \; \frac{1}{\pi}Hz$

primary.subtopicLabel: Fourier Transforms, Frequency Response and Correlation

detailed_solution.concept: Signals and Systems - Fourier Transforms, Frequency Response and Correlation
detailed_solution.markdown:
$f(t)=\frac{1}{2}(1-\cos 2 t)+\cos 2 t$

frequency components are

$$\begin{aligned} f_{1}&=0 \\ f_{2}&=\frac{\omega_{2}}{2 \pi}=\frac{2}{2 \pi}=\frac{1}{\pi} \mathrm{Hz} \end{aligned}$$

pp:ec:2009:q4.title: GATE EC 2009 | Set 1 | Question: 4
pp:ec:2009:q4.question: A fully charged mobile phone with a 12 V battery is good for a 10 minute talktime. Assume that, during the talk-time the battery delivers a constant current of 2 A and its voltage drops linearly from 12 V to 10 V as shown in the figure. How much energy does the battery deliver during this talk-time?

detailed_solution.concept: Network Theory - Basics of Network Analysis
detailed_solution.markdown: $$\begin{aligned} P &=V I \\ \text { Energy } &=P \cdot t=V \cdot|t=(V . t)| \\ I &=2 \mathrm{A} \quad(\text { given }) \\ V \cdot t &=\text { Area under } V-t \text { curve } \\ V \cdot t &=\left(\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 600\right)+(10 \times 600) \\ &=600+6000 \\ V \cdot t &=6600 \\ E &=(6600) \times 2=13200=13.2 \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}$$

PSD of output

$$\begin{aligned} G_{0}(t) &=|H(t)|^{2} \cdot G_{i}(t) \\ &=k \cdot|H(t)|^{2} \end{aligned}$$

output noise power

$$\begin{aligned} &N_{0}=\int_{-f_{0}}^{+f_{0}} G_{0}(f) d f=k \times\left(\text { areaunder }|H(f)|^{2} \text { curve }\right) \\ &=k \times 2\left(\frac{1}{2} b h\right) \\ &=k f_{0} \times 1 \\ &=1 \times 10^{-10} \times 10 \times 10^{3} \\ &=10^{-6} \mathrm{W} \end{aligned}$$

pp:ec:2009:q18.title: GATE EC 2009 | Set 1 | Question: 18
pp:ec:2009:q18.question: Consider the system $\frac{dx}{dt}=Ax+Bu$ with $$A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$B=\begin{bmatrix} p\\ q \end{bmatrix}$$ where p and q are arbitrary real numbers. Which of the following statements about the controllability of the system is true ?
options: The system is completely state controllable for any nonzero values of p and q
Only p = 0 and q = 0 result in controllability
The system is uncontrollable for all values of p and q
We cannot conclude about controllability from the given data

detailed_solution.markdown:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\0 & 1\end{array}\right] \\ B&=\left[\begin{array}{l}p \\q\end{array}\right] \end{aligned}$$

For controllabil itycondition is

$$\begin{aligned} Q_{C}&=\left[B, A B, \ldots A^{n-1} B\right] \neq 0\\ A \cdot B&=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\0 & 1\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}p \\q\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}p+0 \\0+q\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}p \\q\end{array}\right]\\ \text{So}\quad Q_{c}&=\left[\begin{array}{ll}p & p \\ q & q\end{array}\right]=0 \end{aligned}$$

So, the system is uncontrollable for all values of p and q

pp:ec:2009:q21.title: GATE EC 2009 | Set 1 | Question: 21
pp:ec:2009:q21.question: Consider two independent random variables X and Y with identical distributions. The variables X and Y take values 0, 1 and 2 with probabilities $\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}\;  and \; \frac{1}{4}$ respectively. What is the conditional probability P(X+Y=2|X-Y=0)?

detailed_solution.markdown: $$\begin{array}{c} P(A \mid B)=\frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \\ P(X+Y=2 \mid X-Y=0) \\ =\frac{P(X+Y=2, X-Y=0)}{P(X-Y=0)} \\ P(X-Y=0)=P(X=0, Y=0)\\ +P(X=1, Y=1)+P(X=2, Y=2) \\ =P(X=0) \cdot P(Y=0)+P(X=1) \cdot P(Y=1) \\ +P(X=2) \cdot P(Y=2) \\ =\frac{3}{8} \\ P(X+Y=2, X-Y=0)=P(X=1, Y=1) \\ =P(X=1) \cdot P(Y=1) \\ =\frac{1}{16} \\ \therefore \quad P(X+Y=2 \mid X-Y=0)=-\frac{1}{16} \times \frac{8}{3}=\frac{1}{6} \end{array}$$

pp:ec:2009:q22.title: GATE EC 2009 | Set 1 | Question: 22
pp:ec:2009:q22.question:
The Taylor series expansion of  $\frac{sin x}{x-\pi }$ at x = $\pi$
 is given by

detailed_solution.markdown:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)=f(\pi) &+\frac{x-\pi}{1 !} \cdot f^{\prime}(\pi)+\frac{(x-\pi)^{2}}{2 !} f^{\prime \prime}(\pi) \ldots \\ \text { Now } f(\pi) &=\lim _{x \rightarrow \pi} \frac{\sin x}{x-\pi} \\ &=\lim _{x \rightarrow \pi} \frac{\cos x}{1}=-1 \\ f^{\prime}(\pi) &=0 \\ f^{\prime \prime}(\pi) &=-1 / 6 \end{aligned}$$

So the expansion is

$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=-1+(-1 / 6)(x-\pi)^{2}+\ldots \\ f(x)&=-1-\frac{(x-\pi)^{2}}{3 !} \cdot+\ldots \end{aligned}$$

pp:ec:2009:q25.title: GATE EC 2009 | Set 1 | Question: 25
pp:ec:2009:q25.question: Match each differential equation in Group I to its family of solution curves from Group II

detailed_solution.markdown:
P.

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x}&=\frac{y}{x}\\ \frac{d y}{y} &=\frac{d x}{x} \Rightarrow \int \frac{d y}{y}=\int \frac{d x}{x} \\ \log y &=\log x+\log c \\ &=\log c x \end{aligned}$$

Q.

$$\begin{aligned} y&=c x \quad \ldots \text{ Equation of straight line.}\\ \frac{d y}{d x}&=\frac{-y}{x} \\ \frac{d y}{y} &=\frac{-d x}{x} \Rightarrow \int \frac{d y}{y}=-\int \frac{d x}{x} \\ \log y &=-\log x+\log c \\ \log y+\log x &=\log c \\ \log y x &=\log c \\ y x &=c \\ y &=c / x \\ &\quad \quad \text{Equation of hyperbola.} \end{aligned}$$

R.

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x}&=\frac{x}{y}, y d y=x d x \\ \Rightarrow \int y d y&=\int x d x \\ \frac{y^{2}}{2}-\frac{x^{2}}{2}&=\frac{c^{2}}{2} \rightarrow \text{ const}\\ y^{2}-x^{2}&=c^{2} \\ \frac{y^{2}}{c^{2}}-\frac{x^{2}}{c^{2}}&=1 &\text{Equation of hyperbola.}\\ \end{aligned}$$

S.

$$\begin{aligned} \quad \frac{d y}{d x}&=\frac{-x}{y} \\ \Rightarrow \int y d y&=-\int x d x \\ \frac{y^{2}}{2}&=-\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\frac{c^{2}}{2} \\ \frac{y^{2}}{2}+\frac{x^{2}}{2}&=\frac{c^{2}}{2} \\ x^{2}+y^{2}&=c^{2} &\text{Equation of circle.} \end{aligned}$$

detailed_solution.markdown: $$\begin{aligned} 1+G(s) H(s) &=0 \\ 1+\frac{K\left(s^{2}-2 s+2\right)}{s^{2}+2 s+2} &=0 \\ k &=-\frac{s^{2}+2 s+2}{s^{2}-2 s+2} \\ \text{put }\quad \frac{\partial K}{\partial s}&=0\text{ we have}\\ \left(s^{2}-2 s+2\right)(s+1) &-\left(s^{2}+2 s+2\right) \\ (s-1) =0 \\ 2 s^{2}-4 s^{2}+4 &=0 \\ 2 s^{2} &=+4 \\ s &=\pm \sqrt{2} \\ \text{Angle of departure is}\\ \phi_{D}=\phi\\ \text { where } &=\Sigma \phi_{2}-\Sigma \phi_{p} \\ &=225^{\circ} \\ \phi_{D} &=\pm 225^{\circ} \end{aligned} \\ \text{No option is matching.}$$

pp:ec:2009:q44.title: GATE EC 2009 | Set 1 | Question: 44
pp:ec:2009:q44.question:
An LTI system having transfer function $\frac{s^{2}+1}{s^{2}+2s+1}$
 and input $x(t) = sin(t+1)$ is in steady state. The output is sampled at a rate $\omega_{s}$  rad/s to obtain the final output {y(k)}. Which of the following is true ?
options: y(.) is zero for all sampling frequencies $\omega _{s}$
y(.) is nonzero for all sampling frequencies $\omega _{s}$
y(.) is nonzero for $\omega _{s} \gt 2$  , but zero for $\omega _{s} \lt 2$
y(.) is zero for $\omega _{s} \gt 2$, but nonzero for $\omega _{s} \lt 2$

detailed_solution.markdown: $$\begin{aligned} x(t) &=\sin (t+1) \\ \omega &=1 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} \\ X(s) &=\frac{\omega }{(\omega )^{2}+s^{2}} \cdot e^{s}=\frac{1}{1^{2}+s^{2}} \theta^{s}=\frac{e^{s}}{s^{2}+1} \\ H(s) &=\frac{Y(s)}{X(s)} \\ Y(s) &=H(s) X(s)\\ Y(s)&=\frac{s^{2}+1}{s^{2}+2 s+1} \times \frac{e^{s}}{s^{2}+1}=\frac{e^{s}}{s^{2}+2 s+1}\\ Y(s)&=\frac{e^{s}}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ y(t) &=(t+1) e^{(t+1)} \\ y(\infty) &=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s Y(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} \frac{s e^{s}}{(s+1)^{2}}=0 \end{aligned}$$ So, at steady state y remains zero for all sampling frequencies $\omega_{S}$

What current distribution leads to this field ? [Hint : The algebra is trivial in cylindrical coordinates.]

Applying $\nabla \cdot H=J$

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla \times B&=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \hat{a}_{x} & \hat{a}_{y} & \hat{a}_{z} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ \frac{-y}{x^{2}+y^{2}} & \frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}} & 0 \end{array}\right|=0 \\ J&=0 \end{aligned}$$

pp:ec:2009:q55.title: GATE EC 2009 | Set 1 | Question: 55
pp:ec:2009:q55.question:
The amplitude of a random signal is uniformly distributed between -5 V and 5 V.

If the signal to quantization noise ratio required in uniformly quantizing the signal is 43.5 dB, the step of the quantization is approximately

detailed_solution.markdown:
Signal power,

$$\begin{aligned} S &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} f_{X}(x) d x=\int_{-5}^{5} \frac{1}{10} x^{2} d x=\frac{25}{3} \\ S Q N R &=43.5 \mathrm{dB} \text { (or) } 10^{(4.35)} \\ N_{O} &=\frac{\Delta^{2}}{12}=\frac{S}{\mathrm{SQNR}} \\ \text{So},\quad \Delta &=\sqrt{\frac{12(S)}{\mathrm{SQNR}}}=\sqrt{\frac{12 \times 25}{3\left(10^{4.35}\right)}}=0.0668 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}$$

pp:ec:2009:q56.title: GATE EC 2009 | Set 1 | Question: 56
pp:ec:2009:q56.question:
The amplitude of a random signal is uniformly distributed between -5 V and 5 V.

If the positive values of the signal are uniformly quantized with a step size of 0.05 V, and the negative values are uniformly quantized with a step size of 0.1 V, the resulting signal to quantization noise ration is approximately

detailed_solution.markdown:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{\Delta}_{1}&=0.05 \mathrm{V} \text { (for positive values) }\\ \Delta_{2}&=0.1 \mathrm{V} \text{ (for negative values)} \end{aligned}$$

The amplitude of the input signal is symmetrically

distributed about zero. Hence,

$P\left(\Delta_{1}\right)=P\left(\Delta_{2}\right)=0.50$

So, the quantization noise power will be

$$\begin{aligned} N_{0} &=\frac{\Delta_{1}^{2}}{12} P\left(\Delta_{1}\right)+\frac{\Delta_{2}^{2}}{12} P\left(\Delta_{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{24}\left(\Delta_{1}^{2}+\Delta_{2}^{2}\right)=\frac{125}{24 \times 10000}=\frac{1}{1920} \end{aligned}$$

Signal power,

$$\begin{aligned} S &=\frac{25}{3} \\ S Q N R &=\frac{S}{N_{0}}=\frac{1920 \times 25}{3}=16000 \end{aligned}$$

In decilogs,

$[\mathrm{SQNR}]=10 \log _{10}(\mathrm{SONR})=42 \mathrm{dB}$

pp:ec:2009:q57.title: GATE EC 2009 | Set 1 | Question: 57
pp:ec:2009:q57.question:
Consider for CMOS circuit shown, where the gate voltage $V_{G}$ of the n-MOSFET is increased from zero, while the gate voltage of the p -MOSFET is kept constant at 3 V. Assume, that, for both transistors, the magnitude of the threshold voltage is 1 V and the product of the trans-conductance parameter and the (W/L) ratio, i.e. the quantity $\mu C_{ox}(W/L)$, is $1mA \cdot V^{-2}$.

For small increase in $V_{G}$ beyond 1V, which of the following gives the correct description of the region of operation of each MOSFET
options: Both the MOSFETs are in saturation region
Both the MOSFETs are in triode region
n-MOSFETs is in triode and p -MOSFET is in saturation region
n- MOSFET is in saturation and p -MOSFET is in triode region

detailed_solution.concept: Analog Circuits - FET and MOSFET Analysis
detailed_solution.markdown:
When  $V_{G}$  is little higher than 1v

For n-MOSFET,

$V_{GSn}=V_{G}=1^{+}V\; \; (1^{+} \text{Little higher than 1})$

$V_{GSn}=V_{Tn}=0^{+}V\; \;  (0^{+} \text{Little higher than 0})$

For  p-MOSFET,

$V_{S G P}=V_{D D}-3 V=2 V$

$V_{S G P}-\left|V_{T P}\right|=1 V$

$\left(V_{G S n}-V_{T n}\right) \lt \left(V_{S G P}-\left|V_{T P}\right|\right)$

So,  n-MOSFET will be in saturation

p-MOSFET will be in triode region.

pp:ec:2009:q58.title: GATE EC 2009 | Set 1 | Question: 58
pp:ec:2009:q58.question:
Consider for CMOS circuit shown, where the gate voltage $V_{G}$ of the n-MOSFET is increased from zero, while the gate voltage of the p -MOSFET is kept constant at 3 V. Assume, that, for both transistors, the magnitude of the threshold voltage is 1 V and the product of the trans-conductance parameter and the (W/L) ratio, i.e. the quantity $\mu C_{ox}(W/L)$, is $1mA \cdot V^{-2}$.

Estimate the output voltage $V_{0} \; for \; V_{G}$ = 1.5 V.

detailed_solution.concept: Analog Circuits - FET and MOSFET Analysis
detailed_solution.markdown:
When $V_{G}=1.5 \mathrm{V}:$

For n-MOSFET,

$$\begin{array}{l} V_{G S n}=V_{G}=1.5 \mathrm{V} \\ V_{G S n}-V_{T n}=0.5 \mathrm{V} \end{array}$$

For p-MOSFET,

$$\begin{array}{l} V_{S G P}=V_{D D}-3 V=2 V\\ V_{S G P}-\left|V_{T P}\right|=2 V-1 V=1 V \\ \left(V_{G S_{n}}-V_{T_{n}}\right) \lt \left(V_{S G P}-\mid V_{T P}\right) \end{array}$$

So, n -MOSFET will be in saturation region and

p-MOSFET will be in triode region.

To determine $V_{0}:$

$$\begin{aligned} I_{D S n}&=I_{S D P} \\ K_{n}\left(V_{G S \cap}-V_{T n}\right)^{2}&=K_{P}\left[2\left(V_{S G P}-\left|V_{T P}\right|\right) V_{S O P}-V_{S S P}^{2}\right]\\ \text{Given that,} \quad K_{n}&=K_{p} \\ \text { So, } &(0.5)^{n}=2(1 \vee)\left(V_{D D}-V_{0}\right)-\left(V_{D 0}-V_{0}\right) \\ 0.25 &=2\left(5-V_{0}\right)-\left(5-V_{0}\right)^{2} \\ -0.25 &=10-2 V_{0}-25+10 V_{0}-V_{0}^{2} \\ V_{0}^{2}-8 V_{0}+15.25 &=0 \\ V_{0} &=\frac{8 \pm \sqrt{64-4(15.25)}}{2} \\ &=4 \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=4.866 \mathrm{Vor} 3.134 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}$$

Check for valid $V_{0}$

We know that n -MOSFET is in saturation region and p -MOSFET is in triode region.

So, $V_{0} \geq V_{G S n}-V_{T n}$

$\Rightarrow$ Both the possibilities of $V_{0}$ satisfies this and $\left[V_{S D P}=\left(5-V_{0}\right)\right] \lt \left[V_{S G P}-\left|V_{T P}\right|=1\mathrm{V}\right]$

For $V_{0}=4.866 \mathrm{V},$

$\left[V_{S D P}=0.314 \mathrm{V}\right]\ lt \left[V_{S G P}-\left|V_{T P}\right|=1 \mathrm{V}\right]$

For $V_{0}=3.134 \mathrm{V},$

$\left[V_{S D P}=0.866 \mathrm{V}\right]\gt \left[V_{S G P}-\left|V_{T P}\right|=1 \mathrm{V}\right]$

So, the valid value of $V_{o}$ is $4.866 \mathrm{V} \text{or }4+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \mathrm{V}$

detailed_solution.markdown: $$\begin{aligned} a&=1 \\ b&=\bar{P}_{2} \\ c&=\bar{P}_{1} & \ldots 1(\mathrm{NOT}) \\ d&=1=c+e \\ e&=P_{1}+\bar{P}_{2} &\ldots 1(\mathrm{OR}) \\ f&=\bar{P}_{1}+P_{2} &\ldots 1(\mathrm{OR}) \\ \Rightarrow\quad g&=P_{1}+P_{2} & \ldots 1(\mathrm{OR}) \\ g&=P_{1}+P_{2} \\ d&=1=c+e \end{aligned}$$
